The Institution of One

I wanted a language model to teach me Tamil. What I ended up with is the six jobs a school does — all six, around one person, for five dollars a month.

Architecture note Derived from one system, one learner 8 August 2026

The thing itself

A tutor for one person, in a dialect no course teaches

Every morning something on my phone asks me a question in Tamil. It chose that question out of what I got wrong last week, and it is waiting for an answer it will grade. In the car it hands me a podcast episode it wrote, cast and rendered overnight, built around the four phrases I keep failing. Once or twice a week it sends me out with a single line to use on my wife at dinner, and asks me the next day whether I did.

There is no company behind this. It is a repository I own, about half of it written by the coding agent I built it with, and the bill is about five dollars a month. The practice is a year old, the repository six months, the part that reaches out on its own since June. What has been going on for a year is the failing, and that is where all six parts came from.

What it teaches is the Coimbatore Tamil my wife's family speaks at home — which no course teaches, and which every translator on earth will quietly convert into something else. I did not arrive with that target; my first dialect instruction said Chennai. Coimbatore came from a person: it was my wife's first correction when I finally showed her the thing. It could not have been specified from the inside, because the gap it encodes is invisible to anyone who cannot already hear it — which is the entire argument for the fifth part below.

The rest accumulated in close to the reverse of the order this note presents — audio first, for a motivational reason before a pedagogical one, and measurement last — and what accumulated has a shape I recognise. Teaching turned out to be a small fraction of the work. The rest of it — knowing where I am, deciding what comes next, making the material, holding the standard, getting it in front of me on a day I would rather not, and keeping the whole thing from drifting year over year — is what a school does. Six jobs, held by six different people, and only one of them is the teacher.

That is why this note is about a university and not about Tamil. Take the school away and the jobs do not go away — they go unowned. What I did not expect is that one person can now pick up all six. What follows is those six jobs, and the thing that broke to teach me each was a separate job at all.

Both repositories are public, MIT licensed

tamil-tutor The system this note describes, still running. Its decision log holds every failure below in the form it actually arrived, along with the fixes that were proposed and refused. Anna introduces himself — 3:59, in English.

Sollu The same machine with my language and my life removed. The coding agent you already use interviews you and writes yours from it.

The class of problem

A goal that nobody is enforcing

Learning my wife's dialect is one instance of something general. Some goals come with an apparatus: a degree has a supervisor, a committee, a submission date and an audience that will judge the result in public — miss six weeks and someone notices. Other goals have none of that: an adult learning a language they are not immersed in, taking up an instrument at forty, keeping up a rehab protocol after discharge. Four properties travel together:

  • Nothing degrades when you skip. There is no penalty to absorb, and the decision to quit never has to be made out loud. It happens by not happening.
  • The reward is months out and cannot be scheduled. You cannot book the day you first follow the conversation at the dinner table.
  • A single session emits no signal. Nothing you can feel changes in twenty minutes, which reads as nothing happened.
  • Nobody is holding the standards. No teacher to say the register is wrong, no editor to catch the error, no committee to stop this year's version drifting away from last year's.

That last one is the tell. The absent thing is not motivation specifically — it is an institution: a bundle of separate jobs, held by different people, that a school performs on your behalf so quietly you only notice once they are gone. Almost none of what it takes to replace that bundle is conversational. The coach you actually talk to is the smallest component in the build.

Where the six came from

Take a school apart and count what falls out

The honest way to arrive at an architecture for this is not to design it, but to look at the institution you no longer have and ask which of its jobs are now unowned. A language class is a good specimen because its jobs are visibly held by different people, answerable to different things — a separation that was there before software was involved.

The teacher's notebook. Who has met what, who is faking it, who needs last month's thing again — and which of them goes quiet if you push.

The learner model

The timetable, the room, the tray you put the homework in. Contact at a time you did not choose, and an answer that gets back to whoever marks it.

The loop and the rails

The tuition already paid, the grade at the end, the classmate who asks where you were. The reasons you are in the room at all.

The motivation engine

The coursebook and the tape. Material made in advance by people who are not you.

The studio

The fact that the teacher actually speaks the language, in the register you need, and can say "nobody says it that way."

The domain pack

The department. The syllabus review, the record of what was tried in 2019 and dropped, the reason next year is not a random walk from this one.

The governance kit

Six jobs, six owners, kept apart for the reason any system keeps concerns apart: they fail differently and are fixed by different people. A registrar cannot fix a bad textbook. A brilliant textbook cannot make anyone show up.

This is a check I ran afterwards, not a history. Four of the six existed as code long before they had names, because you cannot avoid writing them to make the thing run at all; governance and motivation were named last, after the system kept failing in ways the other four could not fix.

One candidate failed the test. Continuity — what happened last week, what is still open — looked like a seventh part and got a schema of its own, but it never failed alone, only ever as a symptom of the learner model. It was cut. A concern that cannot fail alone is not a part.

The one pair everyone collapses

A motivation engine is not a notification system

Both show up as a message on a phone, so they read as one thing. They fail in opposite directions. Perfect rails, no motivation engine: doses arrive on time, correctly rate-limited, scored properly whenever they are answered — and nobody answers them, with every log green. That is the state most personal-agent projects reach and mistake for a delivery bug. Perfect motivation engine, no rails: compelling reasons to practise that never arrive at 7am, and a reply that lands nowhere.

They are also debugged with different instruments. Rails questions are answered in an afternoon with timestamps: did the tick fire, did the gate pass, did the reply match its prompt. Motivation questions are only answerable over weeks: what happened after the four-day lapse, whether the person came back on their own.

The six

What each one is, and the failure that paid for it

Each entry states what the part needs and why, then one thing that went wrong. Every mechanism named here replaced something that broke in a way I can point at.

Each part below carries a link to its own write-up — all six are indexed at the foot of this page.

Learner model

Stands in for: the teacher's notebook

What it believes about the person

What it counts about the person, and what it has concluded about them.

  • Two stores, two owners. Counters the machine keeps — what fires, what decays, what is due — and a notebook the coach writes: how this person wants to be taught, what they called too much, which assignment they called contrived. The counters are deterministic and only a scored answer may touch them. The notebook is prose, and nothing in it could have been produced by a grade. A preference is not a result, and the system that has only counters will keep being correct at someone in a way they will not come back to.
  • Two grades, never one score. Recognising something and producing it cold decay at different rates. Collapse them and the system reports 92 words solid while the person can fire 41. The analogue is everywhere: what you can follow, versus what you can do unaided.
  • An error ledger that retires rather than deletes. Record the pattern, not each wrong answer, and reopen the original entry intact when it recurs. A mistake you believed was fixed coming back is the most informative event the ledger holds. One ordering function decides what it surfaces next, in one place, read by every channel.
What went wrong — silence is not one thing

An expired token killed the inbound reply path for three days while outgoing messages kept arriving. The outage was not the expensive part: every unanswered prompt was written as reply: null, byte-identical to a prompt the learner had read and ignored, so the system spent three days building a portrait of a non-responsive learner. A broken channel and a person who declined must never serialise the same way.

Not the transcript. History is what was said; this is what is believed. The counters move only on a scored answer; the notebook moves when the person tells you something true about themselves. Neither is a record of the conversation.

Deeper: You Knew This on Tuesday

Loop and rails

Stands in for: the timetable, the room, the homework tray

How a dose reaches them, and how the answer gets home

The largest surface, and the part where an agent most visibly behaves like one.

  • Policy in the model, rails in code. The model decides whether to reach out, how and when; code holds the waking hours, the daily cap and the minimum gap, and nothing else. Split it the other way — rules judging relevance, prompts holding limits — and the system is both rigid and unreliable.
  • Silence is a first-class output. "Not now" has to be a decision the system can make and record. If it cannot, it will always fire.
What went wrong — two questions, one answer

Two messages fired in the same tick, and the judge resolved answers by assuming the newest was the question — so a correct answer to the first was graded against the second, and the model moved backwards on a rep the person had earned. Neither half of the fix was a prompt: one unforced message per tick, and an id on every message that the reply must return with, so an answer finds its own question.

Not the motivation engine. Transport and accounting only: did it arrive, did the answer get home, did it score honestly.

Deeper: It Texts You First

Motivation engine

Stands in for: the tuition, the grade, the cohort

Where the pull comes from

Devices that make a payoff months out feel present-tense.

  • No manufactured consequence. Streaks and guilt invent a cost for missing, which makes quitting cheaper than returning. The design goal is the opposite — make returning cheap: no makeup work, no deficit recited back, a partial session counts.
  • Assignments that leave the software. One line to deploy in real life tonight, unprompted, collected at the next contact. A line that survives live use is the strongest evidence of real capability available, and it makes a distant goal briefly concrete.
What went wrong — the assignment that got refused

A mission went out with a line to deploy at dinner and was refused on two correct grounds: no audience — it is a line for relatives meeting you, not a wife of ten years — and no teach, since the phrase had never been shown to him. Two rules now hold: teach a line before assigning it, and aim it at someone who would plausibly hear it. The device was never the problem; the aiming was.

Not notifications, gamification, or persona. Not a tone of voice but a set of constraints every other part obeys — a frame in the diagram, not a box.

Deeper: Nothing Gets Worse If You Skip Today

Studio

Stands in for: the coursebook and the tape

How the material gets made

Generating content that ships without a human reading it first.

  • Narrow passes, not one prompt. Plan, then script, then dialect and integrity. A single generation cannot hold all the constraints and stay accurate; collapsing the passes corrupted the output twice, in two different ways, and both versions read fluently.
  • The writer gets no filesystem. Generation runs sandboxed and print-only: no file writes, no version control, no publishing. A deterministic layer receives the text, saves it, checks it, and decides whether it ships.
What went wrong — the episode that never said it

An episode came back beautifully made — right register, right scene, on topic — and never once uttered the phrase it was commissioned to rehearse. The learner cannot catch that: noticing an absent phrase in a language you do not yet have is the very capability the episode exists to build. So the check is mechanical and sits before publication — every commissioned phrase must appear verbatim or the run stops. Each gate exists because something got through once.

Not the domain pack. This governs how material is made and what stops it shipping; it has no opinion about what is correct — it asks the pack.

Deeper: The Writer Gets No Filesystem

Domain pack

Stands in for: a teacher who actually speaks it

What the model does not know about your domain

A vetted delta between what a model produces natively and what the domain actually sounds like.

  • It is curated content with an owner, not a prompt instruction. Versioned like code, reviewed by someone who knows, and applied where it is guaranteed rather than requested — the pronunciation fixes live at the audio renderer, past the point a model could override them.
  • The informant policy is part of the pack. Who the native speaker is, how they are consulted, and what they must never be turned into: here, sixty-second checks on specific phrasings, never grammar lessons, because turning a family member into an examiner costs more than it buys.
What went wrong — three ways a translator is confidently useless

Morphology: "I'm going" comes back as போகிறேன், pogiren — correct, and nobody in Coimbatore says it; the spoken form is poren. Vocabulary: "market" comes back as சந்தை, impeccable and instantly bookish, where a real sentence keeps the English word and wraps Tamil grammar round it — market-ku ponom. Pragmatics: "hello" comes back as வணக்கம், the right word and the wrong move; the greeting at home is saaptingala? — did you eat.

All three are invisible to every check in the system, because each one is correct. Only a person who speaks it can see them, which is why this part cannot be automated.

Not prompt engineering. A prompt is a request the model may ignore; a pack is content with a version and an owner, applied where the model has no say. It is also the one part you rebuild for a new domain.

Deeper: Nobody Actually Talks Like That

Governance kit

Stands in for: the department and the syllabus review

How the system is allowed to change

What keeps a weekly-changing system compounding instead of churning.

  • A decision log that records refusals. A rejected approach leaves no trace in the code, and a fresh model context cannot tell "we tried this and it failed" from "nobody has tried this". It will re-propose the idea, persuasively. So will you, six months on.
  • Deliberate latency between an idea and a change. When implementation is nearly free, the scarce resource is evidence. Ideas wait until a pattern reproduces; one-offs never become mechanisms.
What went wrong — a mechanism proposed before anyone read the file

One message format took over the outreach channel — four in four days — and my first proposal was a quota, offered before opening a single file. The plumbing had two causes, neither of them volume: a line in the prompt funnelled that message type into one narrow vein, and the outreach memory rewarded the format for converting, feeding it back to itself. The better half of the real fix was a deletion. The quota would have capped the symptom and looked like it worked.

Not tests or code review. Those check whether a change works; this checks whether it should exist.

Deeper: You Already Decided This

The proof they are separate

Change the goal, and watch the weights change

If motivation were really a flavour of the outreach loop, you could not take one to nearly zero and leave the other elaborate. You can. Point the same architecture at a doctoral student's research assistant and the motivation part almost vanishes — not because the work is easier, but because the apparatus is still there: an advisor, a funding clock, a judgement on a date. Point it at a rehab protocol after discharge and the rails go time-locked and hands-free while the studio nearly disappears. Same six jobs, completely different weights — and that is what distinguishes a real separation of concerns from a tidy diagram drawn over a mess after the fact.

A correction worth making in public

For a while I described the motivation work as an accommodation for my own attention, and that framing was wrong in a way that mattered: it made the most portable part of the build look like a personal quirk. The amount of motivation engineering a system needs is set by the structure of the goal, not the wiring of the person. The doctoral student is not more disciplined than the language learner; they are more surrounded.

Software cannot supply consequence or desire. It can supply everything an institution was doing around them — and that turns out to be most of what an institution was doing.

In practice

Which part is broken

The reason to hold the six apart is not tidiness: when something feels wrong, the symptom tells you which one to open. The wrong instinct, every time, is to reach for the persona.

  • "It asked me something I nailed on Tuesday." Learner model A write that did not land, or two grades collapsed into one. Not forgetfulness.
  • "Nothing about it is wrong. It just isn't how I want to be taught." Learner model A preference the notebook never recorded. The instinct is to rewrite the persona — but the persona is not where that belief lives.
  • "Nothing came all day, then two things at once." Loop and rails The gate, the cap or the tick. Answerable from timestamps in an afternoon.
  • "It all arrives fine. I just stopped opening it." Motivation engine The only symptom no log will show. Look at weeks, and at what happened after the last lapse.
  • "Great episode. It never actually said the phrase it promised." Studio A missing check, not a weak prompt. Every corruption becomes a gate that stops the run.
  • "It is all correct, and nobody speaks like that." Domain pack The model's native register leaking through. Needs the informant, not more instruction.
  • "We keep re-deciding the same thing." Governance kit The refusal was never recorded, so the idea comes back persuasive and unlabelled.

The order

If you are building one

The parts are separable but not equally urgent, and some are far more expensive to retrofit than others.

  1. Write down what the system will believe about the person, before any prompt. Two axes at minimum, and decide early which beliefs are counted and which will only ever be prose. This is the schema everything else reads, and the expensive thing to change later.
  2. Make the write path deterministic. State changes go through code, never through a model editing a file. The model chooses; code records.
  3. Build one channel end to end, including the return path. Adding channels afterwards is cheap; retrofitting a return path is not.
  4. Put governance in before there is anything to govern. The decision log and the budgets cost nothing on day one and are nearly impossible to backfill.
  5. Decide how much motivation engineering the goal requires. Ask what would happen if the person stopped for a month, and who would notice. If the answer is nobody, this decides whether the system is still running in six months.
  6. Generate content last, and get a real informant before you do. It is the most impressive part and the least load-bearing.

One rule sits under all six: nothing goes in that is not earned by a specific outcome or piece of evidence. The pieces that felt clever and had nothing behind them are the ones that got cut.

What it costs

Five dollars a month, and one job that is not for sale

The metered bill is about five dollars a month: Claude Sonnet through OpenRouter, covering what to ask and when, the drafting of every episode, and the grading of every reply. Three exclusions, because that is where an honest accounting goes wrong — the coding-agent subscription I pay for anyway; speech synthesis, free only because a podcast for one listener sits under Google's threshold, a vendor's pricing choice that could change with an email; and my time, a year of evenings, the largest input by a wide margin.

Set five dollars against what it replaced. Four of those six salaried jobs — the tutor with a notebook on you, the registrar who owns the timetable, the fee and cohort that make you turn up, the publisher of the coursebook — are now software I own. That comparison is not close, and it is not the interesting part. The other two were never for sale. The material did not get cheaper; it became possible: nobody publishes a coursebook for the Tamil spoken in one district's kitchens, because a textbook has to amortise across thousands of learners and there is no market here — there is me. And the last job is a person, who lives in my house: no amount of money hires someone to tell me a sentence is perfect and that nobody alive says it that way.

So the bargain, honestly: four of an institution's six jobs got cheap enough for one person to own, a fifth became possible for the first time, and the sixth is still a human being who has to want to help you. That last one is not a gap waiting for a better model to close. It is the shape of the problem.

Which leaves the thing I find remarkable, and it is not the five dollars. It is that the capability landed with me — one person, working alone, on a goal no organisation was ever going to staff. That is worth noticing while it is still surprising.

The claim

What I am actually claiming, which is small

None of the six mechanisms here is new. Two grades per item is spaced repetition, decades old. Deterministic writes, sandboxed generation, a decision log that records refusals, budgets enforced in CI, narrow passes instead of one heroic prompt — ordinary engineering practice, and any working developer will find nothing above they have not seen. I did not invent a technique, and I would rather say so plainly than let it be inferred later by someone less generous.

What is new is the assembly and who it belongs to: all six at once, in one repository, aimed at one person's goal, maintained by that person, for five dollars a month. That configuration did not exist a few years ago at any price, and it fell out of a year of trying to get palatable Tamil lessons out of a language model — the least visionary origin story available, and also the true one.

And the evidence is not this document — a good-looking architecture note is exactly the kind of artifact that can be produced by something that does not work. The only evidence is a number, and it is mine: of all the Tamil words I understand, how many come out of my mouth cold, at a table in கோயம்புத்தூர், with nobody helping me. That number moves slowly, and it is the only thing on this page worth believing.

tamil-tutor — the live one
One learner, one language, six months of commits. Every mechanism in this note is in there, and so is every failure the decision log records.
Sollu — the same six parts, with the Tamil taken out
சொல்லு, "say it". Clone it, open a coding agent, and tell it to set up your tutor — your language, your dialect, your level. You supply the domain pack, because nobody can supply it for you. It does not have to be a language: the other five parts have no opinion about what is being learned.

Both are public and MIT licensed. Fork them, gut them, take the two parts you want and throw away the rest.
